title: What is backward design?
description: Backward design plans learning from the desired results back: outcomes first, then evidence, then activities. Wiggins and McTighe's three stages, applied.
shortAnswer: The backward design method is a way of planning a course or program that starts with the results it must achieve, decides what evidence will show those results have been reached, and only then plans the teaching and learning activities. Described by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe in Understanding by Design (1998), it reverses the habit of choosing content first and writing the assessment last, so every activity has a stated purpose.
keyTakeaways: Backward design has three stages: identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, plan learning experiences and instruction.
Assessment evidence is decided before any content or activity is designed.
Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe set out the method in Understanding by Design, first published by ASCD in 1998, with an expanded second edition in 2005.
The opposite, often called forward design, starts from activities and materials and tries to connect them to goals afterwards.
In workplace and compliance training, backward design starts from the obligation or task and the evidence an auditor would accept.

sections.heading: Where does backward design come from?

blocks.text: Backward design comes from Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe's book [Understanding by Design](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED424227), published by the Association for Supervision and Curriculum Development (ASCD) in 1998. The ERIC abstract summarizes the logic: designing for understanding "begins with what teachers want students to be able to do and proceeds to the evidence they will accept to prove that students have learned it. Only then does it turn to how students will learn it."

An [expanded second edition](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED509029) followed in 2005, with an improved unit template and more guidance on framing big ideas and essential questions. The approach is also known by the book's title, Understanding by Design, or UbD.

sections.heading: What are the three stages of backward design?

blocks.text: The three stages are: identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, and plan learning experiences and instruction. Vanderbilt University's Center for Teaching guide to [Understanding by Design](https://web.archive.org/web/20240104180643/https://cft.vanderbilt.edu/guides-sub-pages/understanding-by-design/) (Bowen, 2017) sets out the questions designers answer at each stage.

blocks.caption: The three stages, with a workplace reading of each (original mapping)
head: Stage
Guiding questions (Vanderbilt summary)
Workplace and compliance reading
rows: What should participants encounter, what knowledge and skills should they master, and what big ideas should they retain?
Which obligations, tasks and decisions must people perform correctly, and to what standard?
How will I know if students have achieved the desired results? What will I accept as evidence of understanding and proficiency?
What observation, record or test result would satisfy an assessor or auditor that each person can do it?
What enabling knowledge and skills are needed, which activities build them, and what materials suit the goals?
Which modules, practice and coaching close the gap between current performance and the evidence required?

blocks.text: Stage one also sets priorities. The Vanderbilt guide describes three nested levels: content worth being familiar with, knowledge and skills important to know and do, and enduring understandings that learners should retain long after the course. Writing those results well is covered in [how to write measurable learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes).

sections.heading: Why is it called backward design?

blocks.text: It is called backward because it starts from the end point and works back to the activities, the reverse of how instructors often plan. The Vanderbilt guide describes the usual "forward design" habit of choosing learning activities, building assessments around them, and only then trying to connect them to the goals.

The guide quotes Wiggins and McTighe: courses "should be logically inferred from the results sought, not derived from the methods, books, and activities with which we are most comfortable," and "the best designs derive backward from the learnings sought."

sections.heading: How does backward design relate to constructive alignment and ADDIE?

blocks.text: Backward design and [constructive alignment](/glossary/constructive-alignment) reach the same result from different traditions: outcomes, assessment and activities that match. Backward design emphasizes the planning sequence; constructive alignment emphasizes the fit between the three parts. The [ADDIE model](/glossary/addie-model) is a broader project process; backward design describes how the design phase should be ordered within it. For assessment specifically, [evidence-centered design](/glossary/evidence-centered-design) applies the same evidence-first logic in more detail.

sections.heading: How can a team tell if a program was designed forward instead?

blocks.text: Original checklist: signs that a training program was designed from content forward rather than from results backward.

items: The assessment was written after the slides, by a different person, from whatever the slides cover.
Quiz questions test recall of definitions when the desired result is a workplace decision or task.
Nobody can state what evidence would show a learner is ready to do the job.
Modules exist because a topic "has always been covered", with no result they serve.
Completion of the course is treated as the evidence, with no observation or task-based check.
When a regulation changes, there is no way to tell which activities and questions must change with it.

blocks.text: Illustrative example: a bank redesigning anti-money laundering training starts with the decisions staff must make (recognize and escalate unusual activity), sets the evidence (correct escalation in realistic case scenarios), and only then builds short modules on the indicators and escalation steps those scenarios require.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry builds in the backward order: obligations and outcomes are defined in the framework, assessment points are attached to them, and content is generated only against those points. Content that serves no outcome, and outcomes without evidence, appear as gaps.

faqs.q: Is backward design only for schools?
faqs.a: No. Understanding by Design was written mainly for school teachers, and the second edition addresses educators from kindergarten through college, but the three-stage logic applies to any structured learning. Corporate and compliance training benefit because the desired results, such as safe task performance or correct regulatory decisions, are usually easy to state and to evidence.

faqs.q: What are the six facets of understanding?
faqs.a: Understanding by Design proposes six facets of understanding: explanation, interpretation, application, perspective, empathy and self-knowledge. They help designers specify what kind of understanding the desired results require, and therefore what evidence in stage two would show it. Workplace programs most often focus on application.

faqs.q: Does backward design mean teaching to the test?
faqs.a: No. Teaching to the test narrows instruction to whatever an existing test checks. Backward design starts from the desired results and designs evidence that genuinely shows them, so preparing for the assessment means achieving the results. If the evidence in stage two is weak, the method exposes it rather than hiding it.
